non_timeline_registry.reason: Dido is a legendary founder associated by tradition with the foundation of Carthage in 814/813 BCE. Her personal reign and death dates are not securely known, so she is excluded from year-based map queries.
Hippolyta is a queen of the Amazons in Greek mythology and has no secure historical chronology.
Ragnar Lodbrok is known primarily from later Norse and Danish traditions. His historicity is disputed and he may be a composite of multiple Viking leaders.

Bjorn Ironside is portrayed in later Norse and Danish legendary traditions as a son of Ragnar Lodbrok and a ruler associated with Sweden. A ninth-century Viking leader named Berno/Bjorn may preserve a historical core, but the identification is not secure and no reliable personal reign chronology can be established. ATLAS therefore preserves the traditional Sweden association while leaving all timeline years unknown.

Po Ngbe is reported in a non-mainstream interpretation of alleged Olmec inscriptions as a ruler in Guerrero between about 900 and 600 BCE. The reading and the individual's historicity are not accepted as secure by mainstream Olmec scholarship.
Minos is a legendary king of Crete in Greek tradition. Bronze Age Crete is archaeologically established, but Minos cannot be securely identified as a historical individual.
Agamemnon is a legendary king of Mycenae in Greek epic and later tradition. Mycenaean civilization is historically established, but Agamemnon's historicity is not securely demonstrated.
Yu the Great is the traditional founder of the Xia dynasty, but his historicity cannot be securely established from contemporary evidence.
Dayang Kalangitan is remembered in later genealogical traditions as a female ruler associated with Tondo, but her exact reign and life dates cannot be securely established.
Hotu Matu'a is the traditional founding king of Rapa Nui, but neither his lifetime nor his reign can be securely dated.

Bilqis is the later Arabic and Islamic traditional name for the Queen of Sheba. The Kingdom of Saba is historically attested, but no secure Sabaic inscription independently identifies a monarch named Bilqis, and her personal reign chronology is unresolved.

Dangun Wanggeom is the legendary founder of Gojoseon in later Korean historical tradition. The conventional 2333 BCE foundation date is preserved only as a traditional-year association; it is not treated as a verified reign boundary, and no secure contemporary personal chronology exists.

Moses is the central leader and lawgiver of the Exodus tradition, but no contemporary evidence securely establishes him as a datable historical individual or provides a verified absolute chronology. ATLAS therefore preserves the traditional Israelite association while leaving all timeline years unknown.

Abraham is the founding patriarch of the Genesis tradition, but historical-critical scholarship cannot independently establish him as a datable historical individual or derive a secure absolute chronology for his life. ATLAS therefore records the traditional clan-leader association without assigning a timeline year.

Eri is the ancestral progenitor in Nri and wider Igbo origin traditions. The traditions preserve conflicting supernatural, local-origin and migration narratives, and no contemporary evidence securely establishes Eri as a datable historical individual or supplies a reliable absolute chronology. ATLAS therefore preserves the traditional Nri association without treating Eri as a securely dated historical king of the formal Kingdom of Nri.

Tyrrhenus is a legendary figure in Greek and later Etruscan foundation traditions. Ancient authors preserve conflicting accounts, including the Lydian migration story, and modern scholarship does not establish him as a datable historical founder of the Etruscan League. ATLAS preserves the traditional Etruscan League association while leaving all chronology unknown.

Aeetes is the legendary king of Colchis in the Greek Argonautic tradition, father of Medea and keeper of the Golden Fleece. Ancient literary tradition associates him with Colchis, but no contemporary evidence securely establishes Aeetes as a datable historical ruler or provides a reliable reign chronology. ATLAS therefore preserves the Colchis association while leaving all timeline years unknown.

Bulan (Bwl'n) appears in later Khazar Hebrew conversion traditions as a ruler associated with the royal adoption of Judaism. The conversion itself is historically important, but scholarship disputes its date, the historical layering of the conversion narratives, and even whether Bulan should be understood as qaghan or bek. ATLAS therefore preserves Bulan as a historical-tradition figure of the Khazar Khaganate without assigning a speculative reign chronology.

Kupe is a major ancestral navigator in Māori oral traditions, but the traditions differ substantially over his voyages, relationship to settlement, and chronology. No secure contemporary evidence establishes a datable personal activity interval. ATLAS therefore preserves the Māori traditional association while leaving all timeline years unknown rather than treating the legacy 900–1200 range as a historical Activity.

ʻAhoʻeitu is the founding Tuʻi Tonga of Tongan oral and genealogical tradition and is explicitly given divine parentage in the origin narrative. The often-cited date around 950 CE is reconstructed from later genealogy and assumed generation lengths rather than a securely attested personal reign boundary. ATLAS therefore preserves the Tongan founding tradition while leaving all timeline years unknown.

The Samuel narrative names Achish as king of Gath in the David tradition, while the superscription of Psalm 34 calls the corresponding ruler Abimelech. Scholarship treats Abimelech variously as a title, alternate name, or textual substitution, and no secure independent personal chronology fixes this ruler's reign. ATLAS therefore preserves the Achish–Abimelech Gath tradition without assigning speculative timeline years.

Hiawatha is a central figure in Haudenosaunee confederacy tradition, but competing foundation chronologies do not establish a defensible personal activity interval for him. ATLAS therefore preserves the historical tradition while leaving his personal timeline unknown rather than turning a debated confederacy date into an individual activity span.

Tlingit historical tradition preserves Gush X'een as an early Shtax'heen leader associated with the origin of the Sheiyksh (Shakes) chiefly title, but it does not provide a defensible personal term equivalent to the legacy 1700–1740 span. ATLAS therefore preserves the person and tradition while leaving the personal timeline unknown.

Sardus (Sardus Pater) is the eponymous mythological hero associated by classical tradition with the people and name of Sardinia. Nuragic civilization is archaeologically historical, but Sardus is not securely established as a historical individual and no defensible personal chronology exists.

Yennenga is a central princess and warrior in Mossi foundation traditions and the mother of Ouedraogo, the dynastic ancestor associated with the Mossi kingdoms. Scholarship warns that early Mossi chronologies reconstructed from oral genealogies are highly conjectural and vary by centuries. ATLAS therefore preserves Yennenga as a founding-tradition figure rather than treating her as a securely dated ruler of a Mossi state.

Joshua is the central leader of the conquest narrative in the Book of Joshua, but modern historical and archaeological scholarship does not support treating the book's unified conquest account as a straightforward record of one securely dated individual's campaigns. ATLAS therefore preserves Joshua as a major biblical tradition figure without assigning a fabricated historical reign or conquest interval.

Taycanamo (often Tacaynamo in modern archaeological literature) is preserved in the anonymous 1604 Chimú dynastic tradition as the founder and first ruler of Chimor, arriving from the sea. Modern archaeological and ethnohistorical scholarship treats the account as a legendary founder tradition and cautions against converting the surviving dynastic narrative into a secure literal chronology. ATLAS therefore preserves the traditional Kingdom of Chimor association without assigning any speculative foundation, accession, reign, or death year.
